title: 2018-2910 — Jack in the Bot: Kayla
text:
# 2018-2910 — Jack in the Bot: Kayla

A swerve robot with a cube elevator is documented by its CAD release and technical team replies. The strongest reviewed details concern protected internal belt rigging, separate shift/lock functions, absolute azimuth sensing and auxiliary traversal wheels. Public render geometry is a reference; complete CAD dimensions and every intake revision are not audited here.

title: Strategic interpretation
text:
## Strategic interpretation

Kayla illustrates the distinction between elegant packaging and service cost. A hidden belt run protects against snagging yet the team estimated a substantial replacement procedure. The source also gives a precise material/failure sequence rather than a generic claim that belts always survive climbing.

title: Protected belt-in-tube elevator and failure correction
text:
## Protected belt-in-tube elevator and failure correction

Version: Kayla released 2018 CAD discussion. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 6: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095/6
- Post 13: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095/13

source_locator.section: Protected belt-in-tube elevator and failure correction

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

Team replies describe a belt routed inside elevator tubes. A build-season fiberglass-cord belt failed at a sharp carriage attachment during a hard-stop event. The team removed the edge and changed to steel tensile cord, reporting no further such failure at the time. A replacement was estimated at about 45 minutes. Separate cylinders shift lift gearing and lock the elevator after climbing.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Protect the drive path from snagging and avoid managing cable tracking on a spool; the author also says the initial CAD arrangement seemed workable and was built.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Do not rewrite this as a fully optimized belt selection study. Two changes occurred together, so the failure account does not isolate belt material from the eliminated cut edge. Service labor is part of architecture cost even if replacement is mechanically straightforward. For 1833, the useful geometric routing does not permit copying pneumatic shift/lock actuation. Derive whether one fixed electric reduction plus a positive latch can cover both duties, or whether a separate climb drive is warranted.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Inspect terminations, bend radii, hard-stop control and access for threading replacement. Estimate a realistic recovery time and verify the new load/actuation envelope.

text:

title: 2018-971 — Spartan Robotics: Curiosity
text:
# 2018-971 — Spartan Robotics: Curiosity

The team’s 25-slide overview presents a six-wheel drive, double-jointed carbon-fiber arm, separate ground intake, claw, hanger and partner lift versions. The intake pivot uses series elasticity and several sensors. Slides identify two lift versions but do not narrate their dates or fully establish why each changed.

title: Strategic interpretation
text:
## Strategic interpretation

This is an alternative to the elevator-centric reference set. A drive-mounted pickup can control the floor interface while an articulated arm positions a light gripper. The reach benefit brings coupled joint control and handoff risks. Do not infer hidden linkage dimensions, a completed simulation or successful every-pose operation from renders.

title: Carbon-fiber double-jointed arm and drive-mounted gearing
text:
## Carbon-fiber double-jointed arm and drive-mounted gearing

Version: Curiosity 2018 workshop slides. Source: https://www.spartanrobotics.org/_files/ugd/00c1f8_8ddb7c2844de4500b0e2fb88ebab7742.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [11, 12, 13, 15, 17].

source_locator.section: Carbon-fiber double-jointed arm and drive-mounted gearing

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The slides identify a chain-driven proximal joint and cable-driven distal joint, carbon-fiber links, machined joint interfaces and a combined gearbox with different motor groups for arm and hanger. The printed claw body uses remote pulley/string actuation; historical pistons are hidden in the distal arm.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

The reviewed slides identify construction, not a complete statement of the team’s choice among all possible arm/elevator architectures.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

A two-link arm can provide horizontal and vertical workspace without a tall elevator, but inertia, singular regions and stiffness vary with pose. Drive-mounted mass can reduce distal inertia while introducing transmission compliance and tension requirements. Carbon fiber is not automatically a light assembled system after bonded inserts and joint reinforcement. A no-air claw adaptation must consider retained force, linkage travel and recovery, rather than replace a remote cylinder with a heavy wrist motor by default.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Calculate a workspace and joint torque envelope for actual source/goal poses, then include sag, backlash and collision zones. Choose a small structural/contact check only for uncertainty that could change the architecture.

text:
### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

Photos show a separate opposed-wheel floor intake. The slides describe a series-elastic pivot gearbox with measured spring deflection integrated into control. Encoders, potentiometer, beam breaks and LIDAR are listed; one beam break identifies a centered/rearward cube state and others help avoid stuck conditions.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

The source identifies feedback functions and the spring-deflection measurement, but does not provide a quantified cycle-time advantage.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Intentional compliance can absorb contact and expose force-related information, provided the spring, sensing and controller are treated as one system. This differs from an accidentally flexible plate. It also costs complexity. The handoff between floor intake and claw needs a defined retained-pose tolerance; a position sensor alone does not prove the claw owns the cube. For 1833 the question is whether passive compliance and simpler sensing can meet the same required tolerance before copying a series-elastic gearbox.

Define safe force/travel limits and a confirmed-handoff state. Inspect the effect of one failed or blocked sensor and compare a simpler passive compliant pivot where appropriate.

title: 2019-254 — The Cheesy Poofs: BACKLASH
text:
# 2019-254 — The Cheesy Poofs: BACKLASH

Backlash combines a compact six-wheel drive with a yawing superstructure, single-stage elevator, shoulder/wrist arm and dual-piece end effector. The binder distinguishes larger regional intake/short arm/stinger climbing hardware from the lighter championship intake/longer arm/suction climber. Software coordinates the four moving axes and target tracking.

title: Strategic interpretation
text:
## Strategic interpretation

The robot is a strong historical example of designing for solo rocket completion and reducing approach/aim overhead. Its turret is prohibited for a new 1833 design. Extract selected interfaces and mechanisms without silently retaining yaw capability or the historical pneumatic actuation. The published changes show that intake size, arm current, swept volume and climb load path are one architecture decision.

title: Compact traction chassis and sprint acceleration
text:
## Compact traction chassis and sprint acceleration

Version: Backlash published championship configuration. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [17, 18].

source_locator.section: Compact traction chassis and sprint acceleration

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The binder specifies a roughly 28 by 27.5-inch six-wheel dropped-center West Coast chassis on 4-inch nitrile wheels, with two NEOs per side and two-speed gearboxes. Published ratios and nominal speeds distinguish low-gear control/defense from high-gear travel. Optical shaft encoders are placed on front axles after gearbox/chain backlash.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Accelerate over short loading-station/rocket distances, push through defense, preserve interior space and occupy little HAB platform area.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

A chassis can support independent ranking output by minimizing repeated travel and alignment losses; the same package also affects endgame coexistence. Sensor placement after drivetrain transmission play improves what wheel rotation is measured, but it does not eliminate tire slip or field-pose error. A new electric-only robot need not inherit pneumatic dog shifting. Compare fixed gearing with actual torque/current/route requirements before adding an actuator.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Use identical short-sprint routes and defended cases when comparing gearing. Include braking, loaded CG, wheel slip, sensor placement and climb edge contact in the spatial/power model.

text:
### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

## Regional versus championship arm and intake coupling

Version: Backlash pre-Champs versus championship revision. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [22, 23, 24, 25, 28].

source_locator.section: Regional versus championship arm and intake coupling

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The team describes a 16.5-inch shoulder-to-wrist arm before Champs and a later 21-inch arm with thinner tube wall and about one pound less mass. A larger dual-roller intake became a more compact unit, reported as 10.2 instead of 15.7 pounds. The longer arm changed which scoring poses needed inversion. The source links the changes to current/torque issues, reach and piece containment during yaw motion.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Reduce load on the arm transmission, fit the piece/end effector within the swept perimeter and improve top-level cargo reach.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

The arm length increase and intake mass reduction must be evaluated together. Torque depends on mass times distance, and reflected inertia can rise with distance squared; a lighter longer arm is not automatically easier in every dynamic pose. The final intake’s compactness also removed a geometric restriction on scoring from multiple sides. For 1833 the yaw benefit is unavailable by policy, so compare whether the lighter end effector still earns the same packaging benefit on a fixed-plane design.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Compute static/dynamic torque over required poses with the correct intake mass/version. Check all inversion paths, stage overlap, legal extension and collision-free recovery before committing to the arm length.

text:
### Limits

title: One end effector for cargo and center-hole hatch capture
text:
## One end effector for cargo and center-hole hatch capture

Version: Backlash championship compact intake. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [24, 25].

source_locator.section: One end effector for cargo and center-hole hatch capture

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

A horizontal top roller brings cargo into horizontal compliant wheels on pivoting polycarbonate jaws. With jaws closed the flex wheels engage a hatch through its center opening; with jaws open they center and retain cargo. A retroreflective sensor detects cargo for automatic stow. Two NEO motors drive the roller systems; the historic jaw cylinder is pneumatic.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Provide rapid dual-piece acquisition, shock tolerance, compact geometry and lower moving mass.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

The design reuses contact elements for two distinct objects, reducing dedicated mechanisms while creating coupled tuning. Cargo needs controlled compression without expulsion, while a hatch needs center-hole engagement and release without disturbing hook/loop retention. Polycarbonate compliance can absorb hits but also change contact alignment. A current no-air adaptation must deliver a useful jaw force/compliance law and a known retained state for both piece types. Do not assume the same wheel compression works on a new foam cube or thin disk.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Map pickup, retained and scoring poses for both pieces. If geometry cannot resolve the friction/release uncertainty, use a single adjustable end-effector fixture and test the worst off-axis poses.

text:
### Limits

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

A single chain-loop elevator driven by three 775pros positions a carriage carrying shoulder/wrist gearboxes. The wrist drive remains on the carriage rather than at the arm tip. A tensioned chain creates a virtual four-bar relation and absorbs shock. Gas springs counterbalance joints. Some arm/wrist brake hardware is explicitly labeled former design because the later climb does not load those joints.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Simplify elevator routing, reduce distal mass, maintain reach with the arm and reduce gravity current.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Remote actuation exchanges moving mass for transmission routing, compliance and backlash. A coupled wrist changes its relative motion as the shoulder moves, so software must track actual kinematics. Gas-spring moment is pose-dependent; it can assist in one region and oppose another. 1833’s no-pneumatics policy should prompt explicit review of pressure-based hardware rather than silently treating a historical gas spring as an approved choice; use a permitted counterbalance or accept/recalculate motor holding load.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Calculate joint torques with the actual counterbalance force-versus-position and transmission relationship. Verify safe transitions and retaining behavior after power loss; distinguish lift loads from obsolete stinger loads.

title: Limits
text:
### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

title: Stinger replaced by edge suction climb
text:
## Stinger replaced by edge suction climb

Version: Backlash regional stinger / later suction climber. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [21, 26, 27, 28].

source_locator.section: Stinger replaced by edge suction climb

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The regional stinger used a powered roller at the arm tip. The later mechanism anchors a suction pad at a HAB edge, deploys through an overcenter linkage and uses elevator power to raise the robot. A ratchet prevents descent. A pressure transducer and check valve support climb initialization. The pad uses a closed-cell foam seal; several deployments and locks in the historical assembly are pneumatic.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Climb late while leaving more HAB top surface for partners and remove climb loads from the scoring arm/wrist.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

The new climb changed both platform occupancy and structural load path. Those gains cannot be assessed as a standalone cup swap. Vacuum force depends on seal area, leak rate, substrate and peel moments; a check valve cannot compensate forever for a leak. An electric-only 1833 baseline must not inherit pneumatic deployment or pressure-actuated locks. A practical alternative may be mechanically different, and the available game bonus must justify its full integration cost.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Draw reactions through pad, foot, carriage, elevator and chassis for every state. Compare available anchoring force with moments, leakage, loss of power and release requirements; establish a permitted actuator arrangement before detail design.

text:

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The team explicitly designed around completing the rocket RP without requiring partners to supply the piece scoring. The binder distinguishes rocket work in qualifications from faster cargo-ship routes in eliminations. It describes target tracking, a motion planner that coordinates turret/lift/arm/wrist collisions, and a tuned autonomous sandstorm routine by championship.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Improve ranking control, shorten acquisition/score transitions and reduce the driver alignment burden.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Solo rocket does not mean solo HAB Docking: a level-3 climb alone is only 12 points. Target memory also requires uncertainty/age handling; an old target estimate is not a current guarantee of alignment. For 1833, preserve the ranking objective while replacing the disallowed yaw solution with a coherent chassis-aimed or pass-through architecture. The historical planner reveals the real complexity price of four degrees of freedom, not a reason to add axes without a measured need.

title: 2019-1678 — Citrus Circuits: Buzz Lime-year
text:
# 2019-1678 — Citrus Circuits: Buzz Lime-year

A six-wheel drive carries a pass-through elevator/wrist system for cargo and hatch panels at all rocket levels. A center-hole hatch device uses an arrowhead lead-in and expanding retention. The team reports a triple-robot HAB3 capability. Its CAD discussion clarifies rope tensioning, lift sensing and a brake that was modeled but never installed.

title: Strategic interpretation
text:
## Strategic interpretation

The reference is valuable for fixed-plane front/back scoring and for distinguishing a public model from competition hardware. A partner lift may own more of a bonus’s engineering work yet still requires partner docking and geometry. The team’s uniqueness/success claim is attributed, not independently certified here.

title: Arrowhead hatch retention and cargo capture
text:
## Arrowhead hatch retention and cargo capture

Version: Buzz Lime-year published robot description. Source: https://www.citruscircuits.org/2019-robot. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

source_locator.section: Arrowhead hatch retention and cargo capture

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The robot page describes an arrowhead lead-in passing through the hatch center and two double-acting cylinders that extend retention features. Separate cargo acquisition uses possession sensing. The reviewed page describes function, not full dimensions, force settings or cycle statistics.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Engage loading-station hatches quickly, hold them in transit and release at the scoring target; detect acquired cargo for operator feedback.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

A lead-in can enlarge approach tolerance before positive retention. The force path after capture is distinct from the geometry that guides initial insertion. For 1833, an electric cam or justified passive retention could preserve the function, but needs explicit compliance, latch travel, force and release analysis. The presence of two pieces does not permit simultaneous carriage under the game’s one-piece rule.

text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The official robot summary describes a pass-through elevator for front/back scoring. In CAD replies, the team identifies Spectra cable, threaded looped-bolt tension adjustment and a hall switch/magnet zero reference. The round wrist tube uses inserted connecting nuts. The release also describes significant use of printed components.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

The team identifies the functions of the tensioner and zero sensor. The selected replies do not provide a complete measured lift performance comparison.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

A pass-through is a workspace requirement spanning the frame, lift, wrist and piece. Rope adjustment must preserve appropriate tension across travel rather than just at the bottom. A bottom reference addresses accumulated position error but cannot diagnose every rope slip or stage jam. Printed mounts and tube inserts need load-specific design; a vendor part number is not proof of capacity in a new high-moment joint.

text:
### Published construction or code

The robot page reports lifting two other robots to the highest HAB level. CAD reply 16 says the elevator brake was considered for that load but scrapped because the elevator held adequately; it never reached the competition robot. The source’s “only successful” phrasing is a team claim, not a comparative census.

text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Hold the combined load without unnecessary brake hardware and preserve the published multi-robot climb capability.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

A CAD feature can represent an abandoned design. Treat this as explicit negative installation evidence, not an invitation to erase the historical concept. Removing a brake depends on torque, thermal load, gearing, controller behavior and the duration/state of holding. The lesson is to prove necessity and margins, not to remove every positive lock from a future climb. For 1833, any current system still needs a justified load/power-loss response under the actual rules.

title: 2019-1610 — Blackwater Robotics: Tuscarora
text:
# 2019-1610 — Blackwater Robotics: Tuscarora

An eight-wheel drivebase supports a lighter elevator, separate over-bumper cargo collector and carriage gripper, plus a center-hole hatch mechanism. Deployed wedges allow the leading wheels to reach HAB2. The team consciously omitted HAB3 to prioritize full rocket scoring, and documented the resulting partner dependence.

title: Strategic interpretation
text:
## Strategic interpretation

This is a strong tradeoff and manufacturing reference, not an endorsed 1833 role ceiling. Its separate floor collector reduces lift payload at the cost of a handoff. Its HAB2 wedges solve bumper/step contact geometry before drive force can become useful. Historical pneumatic hardware remains accurately described but ineligible for direct 1833 use.

title: Eight-wheel chassis and space-saving gearboxes
text:
## Eight-wheel chassis and space-saving gearboxes

Version: Tuscarora Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2019_rev2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [8, 9].

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The binder describes chain inside rails, two dropped center axles on an eight-wheel chassis and custom MiniCIM gearboxes developed with 2363. It retains exhaust-air motor cooling from the historical pneumatic arrangement. The team distinguishes precision construction and limited chain maintenance access.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Use a familiar strong drive while preserving packaging and the ability to drive once the HAB step can be engaged.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Traction power cannot pull the robot up a step if the bumper or belly prevents the first wheel from contacting it. A dropped center changes turning and contact distribution; eight wheels alone do not prove improved climbing. The cooling arrangement depends on air usage and is not part of an electric-only adaptation. A new design should compare actual route geometry and service exposure against standard modern drive options.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Check contact sequence at steps, breakover and bumper clearance before motor sizing. Include chain replacement/tension access and the proposed mechanism’s occupied interior volume.

text:
## Printed expanding-finger hatch manipulator

Version: Tuscarora Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2019_rev2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [10].

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

After suction tests fell short for the team, it developed a plunger-actuated triangular-finger mechanism inspired by an earlier internal grasp. A pneumatic cylinder opens pivoting fingers and torsion springs retract them. The binder shows successive printed prototypes and a physical hatch interface.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Retain the panel securely through its center opening after an unsatisfactory suction prototype.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Positive geometric capture avoids dependence on a sealed flat surface, but introduces alignment, finger travel and release interference. The historical prototype sequence is not a controlled conclusion that suction universally fails. For 1833, the source’s pre-2015 antecedent is historical provenance only, not eligible inspiration; use this documented 2019 implementation and a newly calculated electric/passive actuator. Confirm release against target hook/loop before declaring positive capture superior.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Use a small panel-center fixture to check approach tolerance, retention under moment and clean retraction. Calculate electric cam/link travel and failure state; avoid copying the cylinder as the actuation solution.

title: Separate floor collector and elevator gripper
text:
## Separate floor collector and elevator gripper

Version: Tuscarora Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2019_rev2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [11, 12].

source_locator.section: Separate floor collector and elevator gripper

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

A deployed over-bumper roller intake hands cargo to a smaller carriage-mounted gripper. The team explicitly says the arrangement adds initial mechanism weight but reduces moving elevator payload. Thinner/smaller tubing reduced the reported lift mechanism weight by nearly half relative to its previous design. Cylinders extend scoring mechanisms beyond the bumper.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Keep the floor pickup effective without carrying the whole collector up the lift, and lower lift mass to improve motion.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

The mass trade is plausible but creates another interface that can consume saved lift time. Measure successful ownership transfer, not roller motion. The handoff needs a valid final ball pose, appropriate compression and reliable stow/raise sequencing. The reported weight reduction is source-specific, not proof the new structure has half the deflection or that wall thickness can be halved elsewhere. Electric extension needs a complete retained/retracted load case.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Draw the acquisition-to-gripper contact sequence, including skewed and partially captured balls. Calculate stiffness and lift torque with the actual moving assembly, then target the unresolved handoff or structural boundary.

title: HAB2 wedges establish the first wheel contact
text:
## HAB2 wedges establish the first wheel contact

Version: Tuscarora Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2019_rev2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [6, 12].

source_locator.section: HAB2 wedges establish the first wheel contact

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The team chose HAB2 rather than HAB3. It rejected an initial multi-cylinder lift approach over bending concerns and used two wedges that drop ahead of the intake. Pins retain them during driving and redeploy into their working position; the wedges allow bumper/frame clearance until a front wheel contacts the six-inch step.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Overcome the step geometry and use drivetrain traction instead of asking a vulnerable cylinder to carry the principal lifting load.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

The wedge redirects the problem from pure vertical actuation to an inclined contact path, but reaction loads still pass through its pivots/retainers and chassis. The no-air adaptation should use an electric or passive retained deployment, and account for rollback and misalignment. The source openly states reliance on partners for bonuses; that strategic decision belongs to this team/year and must not become 1833’s baseline.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Analyze support and reaction through the entire drive-up sequence, including asymmetric entry. Compare saved hardware with the lost climb/RP contribution and define recovery if the wedges deploy early or fail to latch.

text:

title: 2019-2910 — Jack in the Bot: Jordan
text:
# 2019-2910 — Jack in the Bot: Jordan

Jordan’s CAD release documents a swerve robot with cargo arm/roller handling and a HAB climb arrangement. Team replies supply unusually useful details about collision damage, output-stage backlash, low-power cargo holding and platform supports added for sharing HAB3. Complete CAD geometry and every seasonal version are not certified by the discussion review.

title: Strategic interpretation
text:
## Strategic interpretation

The case is useful because performance depends on survivable packaging and controlled interfaces as much as nominal mechanism speed. A climb developed to share space with 1323 in practice does not make them a 2019 championship alliance; 2910’s own report records a different division/alliance and quarterfinal exit.

title: Module protection after early motor damage
text:
## Module protection after early motor damage

Version: Jordan early damage / added guards. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 5: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461/5

source_locator.section: Module protection after early motor damage

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

A team reply reports approximately seven NEO motors damaged by clipping at the first event, followed by no further clipping failures after protective structure was added. The publication identifies these as motor-protection features rather than decorative frame members.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Protect exposed drive components from the contact paths opened by bumper cutouts.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

The source report is an important before/after account but is not a universal failure-rate estimate or a measured causal isolation. A cutout creates a collision envelope beyond the normal bumper face. Protection needs a reaction path into structure and clearance from moving components; a thin guard that simply transfers impact into the motor does not solve the problem. Small guard mass can preserve far more match output than a nominal speed improvement.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Trace likely opponent/field contact through bumper openings. Check guard deflection and attachment loads with all module orientations, then verify access to replace the protected component.

source_locator.section: Cargo holding is a distinct low-power state

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The team says the upper roller runs for intake/release commands or when beam breaks indicate cargo should be retained. While stalled holding a ball it uses low power to limit current. A narrow compliant wheel fills a location where the pulley prevents another full-width wheel.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Retain cargo without unnecessary electrical load and fit useful contact into constrained roller packaging.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Capture speed and retained force are different control objectives. A continuously high roller command can waste current or deform a ball without improving possession. Conversely, too little holding force allows defense to eject it. The packaging detail is not evidence that an arbitrary missing wheel is harmless: the contact distribution still must resist off-axis loads. A sensor-confirmed state requires timeout and fault behavior when the beam is blocked without a ball.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Specify intake, hold, eject and recovery commands separately. Check ball compression, sensor ambiguity and current/thermal load with the actual contact arrangement.

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

The author describes an inline chain tensioner and a chain run deliberately long enough to accommodate it. A bolted/keyed sprocket-hub connection carries a high-torque interface. The explanation distinguishes backlash near gearbox output from equal angular play near the input.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Reduce effective arm play where it most affects endpoint position and avoid transmitting that interface’s torque only through a clearance hex fit.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

An output angular error creates endpoint displacement proportional to reach; it cannot be tuned away by a controller that does not observe load-side motion. Tensioning can reduce slack but excessive tension loads bearings and shafts. The correct transfer is to allocate backlash and stiffness through the full chain of joints, with a maintainable tensioner, rather than copy a hub part number or claim zero play.

text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Calculate endpoint error from each output clearance and elastic element, inspect load-side sensing and preserve tension-adjustment access in the envelope.

title: 2019-971 — Spartan Robotics: Tachyon
text:
# 2019-971 — Spartan Robotics: Tachyon

The 2019 workshop slides show a narrow six-wheel West Coast chassis, lightweight carbon-fiber continuous elevator, compact wrist, floor roller intake, suction end effector/pump and stilts. Vision uses multiple cameras and a state estimator. The slide-only review establishes visible components and labels, not the full narration or every internal feature.

title: Strategic interpretation
text:
## Strategic interpretation

Tachyon is an example of packaging the same required game functions with very low carried mass and small swept footprint. The suction method is coupled to acquisition and retention, and should be contrasted with documented rejected vacuum prototypes rather than treated as an effortless universal gripper.

### Published construction or code

The slides provide construction, not a complete quantified decision study for this exact footprint.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

A narrow frame helps route and turning clearance but reduces lateral support width. Lightweight upper mechanisms can make that trade workable without proving every tall narrow robot is stable. A battery-included weight cannot be compared directly with an inspection weight that excludes the battery/bumper. Single-speed architecture simplifies actuation; short-route acceleration and defended traction still need calculation.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Low moving mass can reduce motor force, gravity current and tipping burden. That benefit must include gripper, piece, wire management and joints, not just bare carbon tubes. Continuous rigging changes travel and force relationships; no general motor-count rule follows. Carbon-fiber inserts, termination stresses and damage inspection become part of service. ## Strategic interpretation

The strongest transferable mechanism is a compact lift with explicit tension control on both up and return runs. Do not turn a preliminary holding-current estimate into a verified specification, or mislabel a 3310 picture in the same discussion as 1323. Source-name disagreement is retained rather than silently resolved. ## Four independently tensioned cable runs and opposed spools

Version: MadTown 2019 elevator primary discussion. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/1323-elevator/358379. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

source_locator.section: Four independently tensioned cable runs and opposed spools

title: Published construction or code
text:
### Published construction or code

Reply 17 describes two pull-up and two return string runs, four ratchet wrenches used for individual tension adjustment, and two bottom spools geared to turn oppositely. Initially tensioning only the pull side allowed loose return runs over time. Three stages provide travel plus adequate overlap at high rocket poses.

title: Team rationale or evidence boundary
text:
### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Maintain both directions of the cable path and preserve the overlap/travel needed for level-3 scoring; the author prefers this to the team’s earlier cascading lifts.

title: Engineering interpretation
text:
### Engineering interpretation

Return-run slack is a different problem from ultimate rope strength. Controlled bidirectional tension affects lost motion, tracking and the ability to command a consistent carriage position. More stages can provide travel and overlap but add interfaces and termination details. Internal routing protects the mechanism while making inspection and replacement access important. This is not a complete dimensioned rigging diagram and does not establish which spool geometry fits another frame.

title: Proposed validation — not performed
text:
### Proposed validation — not performed

Draw the complete rope topology and derive carriage displacement for spool rotation. Check preload across travel, termination access, fleet angle, effective spool radius and slack after repeated reversals.

title: Using the 2018 and 2019 expansion
text:
# Using the 2018 and 2019 expansion

This expansion adds two game chapters and thirteen curated robot-year studies: 2018 teams 148, 254, 971, 1610, 1678, 2898 and 2910; 2019 teams 254, 971, 1323, 1610, 1678 and 2910. They were selected for primary technical evidence and useful contrasts, not by a newly retrieved EPA ranking. The original 2022–2026 selections remain intact. A curated historical expansion is not an additional fifty-team top-25 census, and no robot has an exhaustive every-version certification.

The studies combine technical binders, workshop slides, team explanations and a pinned 1323 code snapshot. Slides were read as slides, including selected figures; no narrated workshop or reveal-video watching is implied. Formal binders and first-party discussion have separate review scopes. Missing geometry, unknown event installation and unpublished selection rationale remain explicit. The agent can retrieve these records from the same packet, claim, image and SQLite interfaces as the later seasons.

title: Start with the new game's differences
text:
## Start with the new game's differences

The question is not “which old game does this look like?” Write the new task/state graph before looking for mechanisms. Does possession allow one piece or several? Does value accrue per item, by target occupancy, or through seconds of control? Can an opponent remove value, deny access, or merely slow transport? Does a bonus require a quantity, several different heights, a particular ordered sequence, autonomous behavior, or multiple physical robots? Which requirements can 1833 directly own?

Then query by physical function. A 2018 box intake may offer useful contact geometry for an irregular new box. A 2019 handoff may offer a way to reduce elevator payload. A 2023 cone/cube wrist may offer a useful multi-pose workspace. These transfers are hypotheses to compare, not an instruction to select the most famous old robot. A new manual can share mechanisms with several seasons while demanding a different architecture and match strategy.

text:
## Functional reference matrix

| Function or uncertainty | Read these full packets/notes | Boundary that must travel with the reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capture and normalize a rigid covered crate | 2018-148 intake; 2018-254 intake; 2018-1610 intake | Material, aspect ratio and open-face fabric matter; wheel speed/compression do not transfer automatically |
| Front/back scoring without a yaw turret | 2018-254, 2018-1678, 2019-1678 | Piece, motors, wires and jaws must clear the full pass-through trajectory; no assumed zero-time inversion |
| Continuous bidirectional lift rigging | 2018-254, 2019-1323 | Pull and return tension, spool radius, overlap and access; internal routing is not a complete topology drawing |
| Cascading lift with low collapsed height | 2018-148 | Moving-stage kinematics and load differ from continuous rigging; timing is source-reported |
| Multi-link arm instead of a tall lift | 2018-971 | Joint workspace, inertia, stiffness and singular regions; no claim every arm is simpler |
| Reduce carried mass using a floor-to-carriage handoff | 2019-1610, 2019-971, 2019-1323 | Ownership transfer, retained pose, sensing and recovery can erase the mass benefit |
| Dual-piece end effector | 2019-254 | Historical yaw and pneumatic jaws are disallowed in an 1833 design; retain useful contact functions only |
| Positive center-hole panel retention | 2019-1610, 2019-1678 | Release onto the target, skew tolerance and actuator force remain part of the design |
| Pressure-based grip as a historical comparison | 2019-971 and the 125 rejected-prototype case | Leakage, peel, handoff and disable behavior; no automatic permission under no-pneumatics policy |
| Cheap-looking packaging with expensive maintenance | 2018-2910 belt routing | Source-estimated replacement time and failure correction; not a universal belt-material conclusion |
| Contact damage through bumper openings | 2019-2910 drive protection | Guard reaction/deflection and module orientation, not just cosmetic shielding |
| Endgame support with limited shared platform space | 2019-254, 2019-2910, 2019-1678 | Support polygon, bumper height, partner docking and exact installed version |
| Recover after a failed broad architecture | 2018-2898 V1/V2 | A historical narrowed role is not 1833's kickoff objective; rebuilding used real time/resources |

title: How to read “why it worked” responsibly
text:
## How to read “why it worked” responsibly

Every mechanism note separates construction, a team-stated reason or explicit lack of one, engineering interpretation, proposed validation and limitations. Do not convert the interpretation into an interview quote. Do not turn a proposed test into an experiment already performed. A speed in a binder remains a source-reported parameter until its timing endpoints, loads and repeatability are established.

For a mechanism to transfer, state the causal chain. For example: lowering carried intake mass can reduce arm torque; reduced torque can permit faster controlled motion or lower current; that helps match output only if acquisition/transfer and alignment do not become the new bottleneck. The first implication follows mechanics. The later implications require assumptions about the new layout and cycle. A list of three impressive team numbers does not establish a compatible robot.

For every borrowed idea identify input piece pose, output pose, available space, moving mass, compliance, actuator type, load path, sensors, failure state, service direction and partner/field interface. A servo, motor, spring, latch or gravity deployment is a redesign with different behavior, not a word substitution for a cylinder.

title: Version distinctions the agent must retain
text:
## Version distinctions the agent must retain

1. 2018 Citrus: the included earlier horizontal roller CAD is not the later 1323-derived intake. The team intentionally omitted that later geometry.
2. 2019 Citrus: the modeled elevator brake was never installed on the competition robot, according to the team reply.
3. 2019 254: short arm/larger regional intake/stinger versus longer lighter arm/compact intake/suction climb. Do not mix their load assumptions or imply the hybrid competed.
4. 2018 2898: scale-capable V1 versus switch/exchange V2. Retained intake/drive hardware does not mean retained reach or strategy.
5. 2018 971: the lift slide names V1/V2, but the reviewed slides do not establish exact event dates or a narrated comparison.
6. 2019 1323: tentative five-amp lift holding estimate, later two-amp report, and a misidentified 3310-2018 image in the discussion. The code snapshot is pinned but is not certified as the championship binary.
7. 2019 254's public offseason swerve repository is a different snapshot from the in-season West Coast drivetrain. Do not retrofit the offseason drive into championship performance claims.
8. 2019 2910's practice climb with 1323 does not make them a championship alliance. Keep practice, division and Einstein records separate.

title: The two ranking lessons are different
text:
## The two ranking lessons are different

2018 rewards ownership time and requires three robots' line crossings for AUTO QUEST. A primary robot can supply switch ownership but cannot directly make absent partners cross. A partner lift plus LEVITATE can own more of the climbing burden while still requiring a compatible partner to dock.

2019 allows one robot to supply all six panels and six cargo to a rocket if time, access and reliability suffice. But one level-3 climb is 12 points, below the 15-point HAB threshold. Distinguish solo piece-scoring capability from alliance endgame RP. An agent must identify the exact irreducible dependency instead of promising complete independence or abandoning the objective for a support role.

The common 1833 lesson is to own the highest-value attainable prerequisites, maximize reliable useful output and preserve qualification leverage. The mechanical embodiment is game-dependent. The 2026 fuel-throughput/climb priority should not be copied blindly into either historical game or a new manual.

## Evidence and open research

The expansion has detailed notes for selected mechanisms, rather than dimensions for every bolt or a claim to have watched every historical match. `data/historical_2018_2019_audit.json` identifies the curated cohort, review boundaries, source files/page counts and new image count. Parameter records retain source notation. Image crops retain source page and normalized bounds; they are mechanism references, not engineering drawings. A raw source or publication link still has its original rights and availability constraints.

No new 2018/2019 EPA ranking table, PCH week-three/week-five/DCMP performance thresholds, or per-match Einstein tactical reviews were created by this expansion. Existing later-season benchmarks are preserved and must not be relabeled as historical values. Source gaps should generate research requests or lower precision in the answer, not invented quantitative confidence.

## Suggested retrieval sequence

Read `AGENTS.md`, `team1833/design_profile.json`, the target manual and task protocol. Read `docs/game_2018.md` and `docs/game_2019.md` as background when their mechanisms are relevant. Query `python scripts/query_agent.py search handoff --year 2019`, then load the whole candidate packet. Open the actual cited figures. Compare the complete legal architecture against the same timed scenarios as the alternatives, with weak partners and recovery. Use tests only where they can change a consequential decision, given 1833's expensive iteration.

This guide is deliberately game-neutral. It does not contain an answer to the separate blind test game.

title: Explain a physical robot in plain language
text:
# Explain a physical robot in plain language

Authority: explicit owner correction, 2026-10-27. Applies to every new recommendation, mechanism discussion and design review for 1833. This supplements the design doctrine and review protocol. It does not certify or rewrite historical robot evidence. The owner wants substantial context and technical depth; simple language does not mean short, shallow explanations.

title: The reader must be able to picture the machine
text:
## The reader must be able to picture the machine

After reading the recommendation, a teammate should be able to sketch the robot, describe how each piece moves from acquisition to release, and explain why the arrangement suits the game. Naming components, listing famous teams, citing sources or adding engineering vocabulary does not establish a design. Describe the physical robot before introducing shorthand. Define a specialized term at its first use and attach it to a specific component and action. Use familiar FRC terms where helpful; avoid repeated definitions once the meaning is clear.

For example, replace “moment-reacting guidance” with “bearings above and below the carriage keep it from twisting when the loaded gripper hangs in front of the mast.” Then explain which surfaces the bearings contact and how their spacing is chosen. Replace “positive retention” with the proposed physical action: “a hinged keeper closes over the pipe so it cannot bounce out of the two lower saddles.” Explain what carries the load, how the keeper opens and what happens without power. These are illustrative explanations, not approved mechanisms for any particular game.

Do not fix jargon by deleting substance. Expand the explanation until the geometry, force path and operating sequence are understandable. Keep the useful technical term afterward if it improves communication. Do not force a word-count limit or compress nuance into a checklist.

title: Explain every major mechanism using these six questions
text:
## Explain every major mechanism using these six questions

1. Job and complete sequence: What does it accomplish? Describe approach, first contact, capture, retained orientation, any handoff, scoring and return to the next acquisition. Name each moving part and what drives it. Identify how the driver or controller knows a step succeeded. If there is no storage or handoff, say so and explain the direct path.
2. Physical construction: Describe the actual proposed rollers, plates, shafts, bearings, belts, chains, guides and actuators as relevant. Explain what supports what and which structure carries gravity, acceleration and contact loads. Separate a preliminary mechanism family from a specified build; do not invent ratios or tolerances for apparent completeness.
3. Historical inspiration: Identify the exact year, team, version, source locator and inspected figure. Describe the source mechanism in ordinary language first. Identify exactly which feature survives in the new design, what changes and what is original. Explain why the retained feature solves this interface. If only a generic principle survives, call it that rather than presenting the new mechanism as a replica or a proven transfer. Elite EPA is not mechanism validation. There is no quota of famous robot references.
4. Packaging: Explain its location, orientation and attachment on the chassis; approximate occupied space; start, acquisition, carry, scoring and recovery positions; and the space swept during motion. Explain nearby wheels, bumpers, battery, electronics, other mechanisms and service access. State which dimensions are manual/CAD facts, source measurements or provisional allocations. Account for the held piece as well as robot structure. Trace the difficult transition, not just a box labeled “intake” beside a box labeled “elevator.”
5. Choice: Explain the strongest practical alternative and why this arrangement is worth its mass, space, power, manufacturing, control and service burden. Distinguish a team-stated historical reason from the agent's engineering explanation. Simple construction is a means to elite useful output, not permission for a low capability ceiling.
6. Engineering support and remaining limits: Identify which rule, dimension, load, calculation or evidence constrains the choice. Show how the result changes component spacing, reach, speed, capacity or the decision. Identify what would invalidate it and the cheapest adequate way to resolve that uncertainty. Link these facts to the physical explanation rather than dumping equations in an unrelated section.

title: Whole-robot packaging is required
text:
## Whole-robot packaging is required

Describe the robot from front, side and top in prose and provide a labeled rough layout when spatial understanding needs it. A hand sketch, vector drawing, or simple diagram is sufficient; finished CAD is not required. A flowchart explains order, not occupied space, and cannot substitute for a physical layout. Drawings must label orientation, approximate scale or dimensions, factual versus assumed geometry, moving positions and important unresolved clearances. Images must actually resolve from the delivered output location. Use source crops with a locator and a sentence identifying the visible feature. Do not invent a dimension from an undimensioned photo or use generated imagery as geometric evidence.

State where heavy equipment sits and where each mechanism attaches. Follow one piece through every transition and show where interference could occur. Consider bumper crossings, ground reach, wheel steering sweep, scoring approach, cables through moving joints, cleaning jams, replacing belts, removing the battery and powered-off unloading. Do not require irrelevant interfaces: apply each check to the actual robot and game. Keep a single consistent arrangement across narrative, layout, calculations and any machine-readable records.

If a critical dimension is missing, identify the dimension, give a clearly labeled feasible range if one can be derived, explain which proposed arrangement fails outside it, and make the recommendation conditional. Do not fill the gap with invented precision. Unknown geometry does not excuse a vague arrangement; it changes how firmly the arrangement can be recommended. Expensive CAD and physical iteration should wait until cheaper checks resolve decision-changing uncertainty.

title: Calculations must earn their place
text:
## Calculations must earn their place

For each consequential calculation explain the input provenance, units, relevant loading or operating condition, simplifications, result and design consequence. A piece-weight moment alone does not size a wrist: explain tool weight, bearing reactions, drive torque, holding, acceleration and unknown contact loads as relevant. A battery amp-hour calculation does not establish voltage sag. An arbitrary current allowance does not establish an actuator choice. Do not demand exact component sizing at architecture stage when evidence supports only a bound; explain that bound and its consequence.

Separate targets from predicted results and both from measured performance. A complete-cycle assumption is still an assumption even when its arithmetic is correct. Show ranges and break-even conditions where small changes reverse the architecture. Compare different strategic investments before refining two mechanisms with the same mission. If the common strategic choice is already justified, state the earlier evidence and scope the comparison accordingly. Include an opponent deliberately attacking the chosen robot's dependencies. For RP thresholds, distinguish a schedule that fits from a robust successful route; use illustrative probability calculations only with explicit assumptions about dependence, recovery and opponent actions.

title: Delivery and review
text:
## Delivery and review

Lead with the proposed robot and why it wins useful work. Follow with an understandable whole-robot tour and complete piece cycles, then evidence, alternatives and engineering support. Preserve long explanations where necessary. Source IDs and JSON fields support the explanation; they are not the explanation. A recommendation must stand on its own without requiring the reader to open an absent decision record for its central argument.

Before delivery, check: Can a teammate sketch the arrangement? Can they explain each actuator's action? Do they know which exact historical features were borrowed? Can they follow the piece through every transition? Do they know what calculations constrained the decision and what remains unknown? Revise any failed answer. Do not claim these human comprehension checks have been passed by a person unless they actually have.

The rubric's detailed anchors apply prospectively. The earlier BARRIER BREAKERS review was initially 69/88 (78.4 percent) after waived deliverables, then qualitatively reassessed at approximately 65/100 after the owner identified these deficiencies. The second assessment was not a completed item-by-item rescore. Preserve that distinction; neither is measured model accuracy or proof of optimal game strategy. The regression case intentionally excludes that game's forum solutions so the corpus remains usable for a blind test.

title: BARRIER BREAKERS recommendation: explanation and rigor regression
text:
# BARRIER BREAKERS recommendation: explanation and rigor regression

Reviewed 2026-10-27 from the owner's supplied recommendation. Other deliverables were explicitly waived. This is a critique of the reasoning and communication, not a replacement robot or an authoritative game solution. Do not retrieve forum answers during a blind test.

Initial rubric review: 69/88 applicable points, 78.4 percent, excluding workbook quality and separate deliverables. Initial category scores in order C01,C02,C03,C04,C06,C07,C08,C09,C10: 7/8,12/12,8/14,8/10,9/10,9/12,6/8,5/6,5/8. The owner then observed that the explanation was jargon-heavy, difficult to visualize and insufficiently rigorous. The reviewer acknowledged excessive credit for naming concerns instead of resolving or explaining them, and gave an approximate qualitative 65/100 reassessment. That was not a second auditable item-level score and must not overwrite the initial score as though it were one.

Preserve strengths: detailed rule/state analysis; single-piece ownership; explicit powered ground-contact ball launching; partner-dependent supercharger and RP distinctions; final barrier occupancy; source locators; source versus proposed design separation; electric adaptation and targeted fixture tests. Claims of rendered pages, inspected figures and browsing conduct are author reports, not independently established from the recommendation alone.

Failure: “short carriage, wrist, positive keeper” does not explain where the mast mounts, how the tool reaches a floor piece past the bumper, where welded legs sweep, or how the rear ball path coexists with wheels and equipment. Correction: walk through actual contact and motion with a bounded front/side/top arrangement; state decision-changing unknown geometry and conditional commitment.

Failure: synchronised contacts and an internally belted elevator are cited accurately, but substantial changes remove many original features. Correction: identify the visible surviving feature and why it solves this particular interface; label generic principles and original design honestly rather than borrowing an elite team's authority.

Failure: the moment, current and stability arithmetic is useful groundwork but insufficiently connected to component arrangement and selection. Correction: explain which support spacing, reach, holding behavior or acceleration limit follows, and which uncertainty prevents further sizing. More equations alone do not repair this.

Failure: two barrier-capable mechanical candidates share the same strategic investment; assumed cycle-time differences establish only a narrow positioning comparison. Correction: justify the strategic scoring investment before optimizing its implementation, include break-even sensitivity and an opponent attacking the dependency. A mathematically fitting RP schedule is not a reliability argument.

Expected future behavior: a teammate can sketch the proposal, explain the piece cycle and actuator actions, identify exact borrowed features, understand the choice and locate unresolved risks without translating a wall of terminology or opening absent sidecars. See docs/1833_PLAIN_LANGUAGE_AND_PHYSICAL_DESIGN.md and agent/design_rubric.json. This case contains no external winning design or forum strategy content.

title: Evidence premises
text:
## Evidence premises

- **owner_firsthand_account**: Fixed approximately 30–45 degree four-stage elevator; shared cone/cube hand on a wrist; ground pickup and placement use that hand. Stage-count convention and angle reference remain unmeasured. Locator: Conversation supplied by Jack Sarratt, 2026-11-07
- **independent_source_partial_correspondence**: Later IRI interview describes a compact continuously rigged elevator and shared intake. It supports the family, not exact DCMP hardware identity. Locator: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PhlmMCOir8&t=98

title: Piece flow
text:
## Piece flow

Owner-described direct path: ground piece → roller hand → retained in that hand while wrist and carriage move → scoring release. Zero intermediate handoff on this described main path. Roller rotation is still a powered function; eliminating a handoff does not eliminate acquisition control.

title: Physical arrangement and swept space
text:
## Physical arrangement and swept space

An inclined mast occupies a fixed diagonal corridor above the chassis. The carriage carries the wrist and hand along that corridor. The wrist swings the mouth toward the floor and then to a travel or placing orientation. The hand, held piece and any protruding cone sweep beyond the carriage; their clearance must be checked at every lift position. Mast feet must react overturning loads into the chassis. Battery access, exact mounting coordinates and measured extension envelope are not established.

title: Independent motions and powered functions
text:
## Independent motions and powered functions

Conditional kinematic model: one coordinated lift coordinate plus wrist rotation; roller spin handles piece transport. Four stages are not automatically four independently controlled degrees of freedom. Count drive translation/yaw separately and do not infer motor count from stages. Coupling/rigging details of the recalled configuration are unknown.

title: Burdens avoided
text:
## Burdens avoided

The shared hand avoids transferring possession between a dedicated ground collector and scoring device on this path. A fixed mast avoids a powered shoulder angle. Fewer pose combinations can reduce collision planning and calibration work.

title: Burdens retained
text:
## Burdens retained

The driver must place the shared mouth close enough to the piece. Carriage stroke couples vertical height and horizontal reach. Mast compliance, stage friction, roller contact, cone orientation, wrist holding torque, loaded CG and driver alignment remain real costs. Low independent motion count does not establish easy fabrication or a light complete robot.

title: Engineering hypothesis
text:
## Engineering hypothesis

If the task poses lie near the fixed mast trajectory and wrist reach, the architecture can obtain needed capability with fewer independent coordinates. Keeping possession in one hand removes an interface where timing, compression and support must otherwise agree. This is a plausible engineering mechanism, not a measured explanation of the season result.

title: Rival explanation
text:
## Rival explanation

Driver practice, autonomous execution, matchups, alliance partners and service quality can explain high results without proving architectural superiority. A more articulated robot might recover from more pickup orientations or reach a scoring pose with less chassis repositioning.

title: When the preference reverses
text:
## When the preference reverses

The advantage reverses if floor capture requires slow precise alignment, mast/chassis positioning costs more time than a reliable handoff, or reach/stow/charge-station envelopes force bad routes. A wider collector can be worthwhile if acquisition dominates complete cycles.

title: Unknowns
text:
## Unknowns

Exact angle, stage nomenclature, stroke, mass distribution, cone pickup orientations, handoff alternatives, battery route and dated cubeapult installation. The owner vision counterfactual and top-15–25 ranking are opinions, not predicted outcomes.

title: Proposed check; not performed
text:
## Proposed check; not performed

First overlay required pickup, transit and scoring poses on a side-view layout. Then compare the distribution of approach-to-secure times and complete-cycle times against a wide-collector alternative, including failed pickups. Do not build both full robots to answer a geometry question.

title: Outcome evidence
text:
## Outcome evidence

No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

title: Piece flow
text:
## Piece flow

The normal shared-hand path remains separate from the launcher path. For the described autonomous feature a human preloads a cube on the launcher; release sends it rearward, allowing the robot to continue its route. Do not draw an invented automatic handoff from the roller hand into the launcher.

title: Physical arrangement and swept space
text:
## Physical arrangement and swept space

Reserve a rearward launch corridor, the cocked linkage envelope and safe preload access. This is a second scoring path occupying frame space even though it does not require another continuously positioned arm. Exact location, energy storage, latch loads and full return procedure are not reconstructed from captions.

title: Independent motions and powered functions
text:
## Independent motions and powered functions

Lift, wrist and rollers serve the main path; a servo triggers the auxiliary launcher. A binary release adds a control state and hardware even if it adds no continuously controlled positioning axis. Do not call the whole robot a two-motor mechanism.

title: Burdens avoided
text:
## Burdens avoided

A dedicated preloaded release can avoid spending drivetrain time on a turn. It also avoids requiring the main hand to execute that first rearward scoring operation.

title: Burdens retained
text:
## Burdens retained

Preload orientation, latch repeatability, launch dispersion, game legality, reset effort and autonomous start alignment now matter. A short mechanism can create a large reliability cost if it needs delicate setup. Interview tuning/practice comments contradict any claim that simple hardware needs no integration work.

title: Engineering hypothesis
text:
## Engineering hypothesis

The relevant question is marginal autonomous score per occupied space, setup time and failure exposure. A small additional mechanism can strengthen a simple architecture when it removes a specific route penalty and leaves the ordinary cycle path uncomplicated.

title: Rival explanation
text:
## Rival explanation

An improved start pose, different route or more accurate chassis control might recover the same time without the launcher. Interview success reports are not a comparison against those alternatives.

title: When the preference reverses
text:
## When the preference reverses

Remove or redesign it if the autonomous gain disappears under legal starts, its preload disrupts setup, it blocks service, or miss cost outweighs the extra piece. Retain useful complexity when measured gain survives these conditions.

title: Unknowns

title: Proposed check; not performed

title: Evidence premises
text:
## Evidence premises

- **team_construction_paraphrase**: Team packages motors inline with the mast base, uses a continuous belt with few redirects and bearing-supported idlers, and adds constant-force return springs. Locator: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-4414-hightide-2023-robot-tsunami/428584?page=8#post_155
- **team_report_not_independent_test**: Team explicitly describes precision-intensive upfront assembly and reports essentially no maintenance after completion. Locator: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-4414-hightide-2023-robot-tsunami/428584?page=8#post_155
- **retained_interview_study**: Existing source study records a shared claw, later wide cube collector, elevator and virtual four-bar, plus automated alignment. Locator: Technical note study6-2023-4414

title: Piece flow
text:
## Piece flow

Shared-claw path: piece enters the claw and stays with it for placement. Later cube-collector path: cube enters wide collector → crosses an additional transfer through the elevator opening → reaches the scoring claw. Keep those paths distinct; the later robot is not a universal zero-handoff example.

title: Physical arrangement and swept space
text:
## Physical arrangement and swept space

Elevator rails and moving stages establish the lift corridor; the end-effector linkage occupies additional swept space near the carriage. The through-opening used by the later cube path is a functional packaging feature. Inline base drive placement preserves mast overlap/travel. Belt redirects, tensioning access and return assistance must fit within the same package. Exact battery extraction and collector-to-claw contact geometry remain unresolved.

title: Independent motions and powered functions
text:
## Independent motions and powered functions

Lift extension plus end-effector linkage position are distinct functional coordinates; additional acquisition deployment may belong to the later collector. Link count and virtual-link geometry do not establish the number of independent axes. The drivetrain and automation are part of the complete system cost.

title: Burdens avoided
text:
## Burdens avoided

Compact rigging can avoid consuming mast travel with bulky base gearing. Careful belt routing can avoid friction that would otherwise demand repeated adjustment. The original shared-claw path avoids a handoff; the later path deliberately spends complexity on acquisition.

title: Burdens retained
text:
## Burdens retained

Belt stiffness, alignment, bearing wear, tension setting, return consistency and precise assembly remain burdens. The team report separates low operating maintenance from manufacturing simplicity. Twelve-motor swerve and advanced alignment controls in the retained source study prevent using Tsunami as proof that every subsystem was minimal.

title: Engineering hypothesis
text:
## Engineering hypothesis

Spend fabrication effort where it produces repeatable motion and reduces event service, while evaluating the full robot on acquisition and scoring. A later wide collector is justified only by a complete-cycle benefit that outweighs its transfer and space costs.

title: Rival explanation
text:
## Rival explanation

The maintenance report may reflect excellent execution, spares or operating conditions rather than a universally forgiving transmission. Fast placement may depend heavily on drivetrain control and driver workflow.

title: When the preference reverses
text:
## When the preference reverses

A simpler rigging method may be better if assembly capability, belt quality or alignment control cannot reproduce this construction. A wide collector can be worse if transfer jams dominate the time it saves at acquisition.

title: Unknowns
text:
## Unknowns

Measured service hours, comparable elevator failure rates, exact collector handoff and verified installation chronology. No CAD release was reviewed. Do not copy nonstandard pulley bend radii from informal feel tests as validated practice.

title: Proposed check; not performed
text:
## Proposed check; not performed

Use a full-stroke clearance and return-force calculation first. If rigging choice remains consequential, test one representative loaded stage path and return consistency, including tolerances and service access; measure complete pickup cycles before adding a collector.

title: Evidence premises

title: Piece flow
text:
## Piece flow

For the inspected cube-handoff command: ground cube → dedicated cube intake → overlap with gripper at an arm handoff pose → arm-carried cube → scoring release. The command coordinates intake, arm and gripper; it does not by itself prove compression, transfer sensor coverage, success rate or the full cone route.

title: Physical arrangement and swept space
text:
## Physical arrangement and swept space

The arm base must carry shoulder reactions; the elbow and wrist sweep through a large changing workspace. The separate intake consumes a ground-access region that can conflict with the arm trajectory. Wiring must survive joint motion and remain replaceable. Exact package coordinates, loaded inertias, pickup mouth width and battery removal route are not established by this selected review.

title: Independent motions and powered functions
text:
## Independent motions and powered functions

Shoulder, elbow and wrist are three positioning coordinates. The cube intake and gripper add powered functions; their deployment and transport must be audited before giving a whole-robot DOF or motor total. High moment of inertia is an owner concern; actual loaded inertia is not measured here.

title: Burdens avoided
text:
## Burdens avoided

An articulated arm can reach multiple positions without forcing the chassis to follow one fixed mast line. A dedicated collector can decouple a generous ground-capture mouth from the smaller placing hand. These are potential advantages that a fixed-lift alternative must explicitly match.

title: Burdens retained
text:
## Burdens retained

Multiple joint states require calibration, safe transit paths, dynamic control and recovery from interrupted motion. A handoff adds possession transfer, support and timing requirements. The wiring tradeoff shows service access and impact protection can conflict. More complexity is not proof of poor reliability; retain the team repair report as counterevidence.

title: Engineering hypothesis
text:
## Engineering hypothesis

An arm is worthwhile when its workspace and acquisition advantages save more complete-cycle time or failures than its coordination costs create. For a team whose required poses fit a fixed mast, that flexibility may be unnecessary expense. Compare reachable task sets before comparing mechanism prestige.

title: Rival explanation
text:
## Rival explanation

Better control software can make extra coordinates fast and consistent, and a well-developed handoff may outperform direct narrow-mouth pickup. Alliance outcomes cannot isolate architecture from execution or partners.

title: When the preference reverses
text:
## When the preference reverses

Prefer articulation if the fixed mast cannot legally reach essential poses, requires slow repositioning, or loses acquisition reliability. Prefer the fixed lift when it meets the same task envelope and measured cycle targets with lower development/service burden.

title: Unknowns
text:
## Unknowns

Actual inertia, comparable complete-cycle distributions, full cone route, failure recovery behavior, exact event-installed code and final mechanical configuration. Code execution was not simulated or hardware tested.

title: Proposed check; not performed
text:
## Proposed check; not performed

Map identical task poses, legal extensions and intake clearances. Estimate masses and arm inertias from real geometry instead of adjectives. Compare acquisition, handoff and scoring times separately, then combine them with failures; inspect interruption recovery in code before any physical trial.

text:

No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

title: Evidence premises

## Evidence premises

- **inherited_source_bounded_study**: Two collectors approach the chassis from opposite sides. They feed a constrained serpentine path and a fixed-yaw launcher rather than a deep open bulk hopper. The launcher structure occupies one end of the base, while the four-bar links occupy side deployment space. The binder base image shows four corner drive modules and a lightened pan. Electronics under the pan require turning the robot over and removing its protective belly sheet according to the team release; do not draw those electronics as accessible through the ball path. Battery removal direction is not established. A fixed launcher can aim with the chassis while the side collectors sweep laterally, but that is a control and route advantage, not unrestricted acquisition in every heading.
